chapter_title: Exposing Parameters and Building HDA Interfaces
chapter_summary:
Once you've created a Houdini Digital Asset, the next crucial step is to expose its internal controls to the outside world. This is done by creating *parameters* on the HDA's interface. Parameters are essentially variables that allow users to control aspects of the HDA's internal network without needing to dive into the node graph. For instance, if your HDA generates a procedural tree, you might want parameters for tree height, branch density, leaf size, or even a random seed. These parameters transform your HDA from a static network into a dynamic, customizable tool. Without exposed parameters, an HDA is just a black box; with them, it becomes an incredibly versatile asset.

The primary tool for managing HDA parameters is the **Parameter Interface editor**. You can access this by right-clicking your HDA instance and selecting "Type Properties..." (or "Edit Operator Type Properties..."). This window has several tabs, but we'll focus on the "Parameters" tab. On the left side, you'll see a list of available parameter types (Float, Integer, Toggle, String, Color, File Path, etc.) and interface elements (Folder, Separator, Button). On the right, you'll see the current parameters exposed on your HDA. To add a new parameter, simply drag a parameter type from the left pane to the right pane. For example, drag a "Float" parameter to create a numerical slider.

After dragging a parameter, you'll need to configure its properties. Every parameter has a **Name** (the internal identifier, e.g., `tree_height`), a **Label** (what the user sees, e.g., "Tree Height"), and a **Default Value**. It's vital to use clear, descriptive names and labels. The "Name" is what you'll use in expressions to link to internal nodes, so keep it concise and avoid spaces. The "Label" can be more user-friendly. For numerical parameters (Float, Integer), you can also define a **Range** (min/max values) and a **Soft Range** (the default slider range) to guide users. For example, a "Tree Height" parameter might have a range from 0.1 to 100, but a soft range from 1 to 10, indicating typical usage.

The magic happens when you **link** an HDA parameter to an internal node's parameter. This is typically done using expressions. Let's say you have a `Box` SOP inside your HDA, and you want to control its "Size" parameter (which is a vector, `sizex`, `sizey`, `sizez`) using a single "Box Size" float parameter on your HDA.
1.  Create a "Float" parameter on your HDA, name it `box_size`, and label it "Box Size".
2.  Dive inside your HDA (double-click the HDA node).
3.  Navigate to the `Box` SOP.
4.  Right-click on the `Size` parameter (or `sizex`, `sizey`, `sizez` individually) and choose "Copy Parameter".
5.  Go back up to your HDA node, right-click on the `box_size` parameter you just created, and choose "Paste Relative References". This will automatically create an expression like `ch("box_size")` in the `Box` SOP's size parameter.
    *   Alternatively, you can manually type the expression: `ch("../box_size")` into the `Box` SOP's `sizex`, `sizey`, and `sizez` fields. The `ch()` expression stands for "channel" and is used to reference parameters. `../` means "go up one level" in the node hierarchy to find the HDA's `box_size` parameter.

This linking process is fundamental. You can link any parameter on an internal node to an HDA parameter, allowing you to expose virtually any control. For more complex scenarios, you might use `chf()` for float channels, `chs()` for string channels, or `chi()` for integer channels, though `ch()` often auto-detects the type. You can also combine expressions, for example, `ch("../box_size") * 2` if you want the internal parameter to be double the HDA parameter's value.

Organizing the HDA's user interface is just as important as exposing parameters. A cluttered interface can be confusing and hard to use. The Parameter Interface editor allows you to use **Folders** and **Separators** to group related parameters. Drag a "Folder" item from the left pane to the right. You can choose between "Simple" (a collapsible section) or "Tab" (creates a new tab in the HDA's parameter pane). Drag your related parameters into these folders. Separators (`---`) can be used to visually break up sections within a folder or tab. Good UI design makes your HDA intuitive and user-friendly, which is crucial for adoption by other artists, especially those less familiar with Houdini. Always think about the user experience: what parameters are most important? How can they be logically grouped?

Common mistakes often arise from incorrect linking or data type mismatches. If a parameter isn't responding, first check the expression: Is the path correct (`../` for one level up, `../../` for two, etc.)? Is the parameter name spelled correctly? Second, ensure the data types match. Trying to link a string parameter to a float input will cause an error. Houdini is generally good at implicit conversions, but explicit matching is safer. For instance, if an internal parameter expects a vector (like `(0,0,0)` for position), but you only expose a single float, you might need to use an expression like `ch("../pos_x"), 0, 0` to fill out the vector. Another common issue is forgetting to save the HDA definition after adding or linking parameters. Always "Save Node Type" after making changes in the Parameter Interface editor to ensure your updates are persisted.

screens.title: Exposing Parameters and Building HDA Interfaces
screens.subtitle: Make internal controls visible, useful, and reliable for users

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to turn an internal node network into a usable tool by exposing parameters on a Houdini Digital Asset. Exposed parameters let other artists and scenes drive the procedural logic without opening the node graph. We will show you how to use the Parameter Interface editor to create sliders, toggles, integers, and strings, how to name and label each control for clarity, and how to link those controls into internal node parameters using channel expressions so that the HDA behaves predictably. You will also learn interface organization—folders, separators, and tabs—so the final tool is friendly and discoverable. Finally, we'll cover common mistakes and the critical step of saving the node type so your changes persist. For example, you will expose three float sliders to control a box's dimensions, paste relative references to the internal Box SOP, and then test changes on the HDA node itself. By the end, you will understand why clear names, matching data types, and proper saving make an HDA a trustworthy, reusable asset.

keyIdea.title: Expose to empower
keyIdea.text: Parameters convert internal node settings into a user-facing, reusable interface so artists can control behavior without digging into the graph.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives will guide our lab and practice. First, you will understand why exposing parameters matters: it converts internal node settings into user-facing controls so the HDA can be used without opening the graph. Second, you will gain practical skill with the Parameter Interface editor, learning to add floats, integers, toggles, strings, and file paths and to set defaults and ranges so users have safe, sensible controls. Third, you will learn how to link HDA parameters to internal node parameters using channel expressions or Paste Relative References, including how to reference parent-level parameters and combine expressions when needed. Finally, you will learn interface organization: how to group related parameters with folders, tabs, and separators so the UI is clear and discoverable. Each of these objectives includes a small hands-on step, so you won't just read about changes; you'll apply them to a sample box HDA and verify the geometry updates when you change a slider.

keyIdea.title: Practical, testable goals
keyIdea.text: Focus on adding, linking, organizing, and validating parameters so your HDAs are both functional and usable.

screens.title: Why Expose Parameters?
screens.subtitle: From a black box to a configurable tool

narration.text: Exposing parameters is the act of making selected internal controls visible and editable on the HDA's public interface. In practice, that means you pick a small set of knobs—floats, integers, toggles, strings—that capture the essential variability of your procedural system and place them on the asset's parameter pane. For example, if an HDA generates a procedural tree you might expose tree height, branch density, leaf scale, and a random seed. Those exposed controls let an artist iterate rapidly without opening the network. The definition matters because an HDA with no exposed parameters is effectively a black box; it's reusable only by the creator who knows the internal graph. When you expose parameters, you create a contractual surface: the operator names become channels other nodes can reference. A common misconception is that exposing everything is better. In reality, exposing too many low-level parameters makes the UI noisy and confuses users. Instead, expose the meaningful controls and set defaults and soft ranges to guide typical usage. Concrete example: add three floats for a box HDA to control size and watch how a single interface change scales geometry across the internal SOPs. Takeaway: choose controls that map cleanly to artist intent, and keep the interface concise so your asset is approachable.

keyIdea.title: Expose with intent
keyIdea.text: Expose only the parameters that capture meaningful variation so your HDA remains easy to use and maintain.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Why Expose Parameters?
Definition

Expose selected internal controls as HDA parameters

Parameters are the public variables of your HDA. They let users change behavior without diving into nodes.

Good parameter design balances power and simplicity: expose what matters, hide the rest.

Concrete example
A box HDA exposes three floats for X, Y, Z sizes. Changing those sliders changes the Box SOP's size channels without entering the HDA.
Common mistake
Exposing every internal parameter creates a confusing surface and increases maintenance burden.
Key Takeaway

Expose parameters that represent meaningful, artist-facing controls and set sensible defaults to guide use.

Design considerations
  • Names: concise internal identifiers used in expressions. Avoid spaces.
  • Labels: friendly names users see.
  • Defaults and soft ranges guide typical use while allowing full range via typing.
Analogy

Think of the HDA interface as the instrument panel for a machine: show the essential knobs, hide the internal wiring.

Try this
Add one float to an HDA and paste a relative reference into an internal node; verify behavior before adding more.
Why it matters
A focused interface increases adoption and reduces the chance of user error when artists use your asset.

narration.text: The Parameter Interface editor is your primary tool for building an HDA's public pane. Open it by right-clicking the HDA instance and choosing Type Properties, then select the Parameters tab. The editor presents a left list of available parameter types—float, integer, toggle, string, color, file path—and interface elements like folder or separator. The right side shows the exposed parameters for the HDA. To add a control, drag a parameter type from the left to the right. After adding, configure name, label, default value, range, and soft range. The name becomes the internal operator identifier, so keep it concise and avoid spaces; the label is what users read. For numerical sliders, set a hard range to limit valid values and a soft range as the slider's default span; this nudges users toward typical values while allowing the full range if needed. You can reorder parameters by dragging them and place separators to improve readability. A critical step many forget is saving the node type after applying changes. Clicking Apply and Accept updates the instance, but you must choose Save Node Type on the HDA node to persist the definition to disk. Practice: create floats for box size and set soft ranges from 0.1 to 10 so the slider feels natural; then save the node type.

keyIdea.title: Drag, configure, save
keyIdea.text: Use drag-and-drop to add controls, tune names and ranges, then save the node type so changes persist across sessions.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Parameter Interface Editor
Step-by-step
  1. Open Type Properties and go to the Parameters tab.
  2. Drag a parameter type from the left to the right pane.
  3. Configure Name, Label, Default, Range and Soft Range.
  4. Organize Reorder, add folders and separators.
  5. Apply & Save Apply to instance, then Save Node Type to persist.
Pro tip
Use clear names for expressions and friendlier labels for users. Soft ranges guide typical behavior without hard limiting power.
Parameter properties
Name
Internal identifier used by expressions. Keep concise and avoid spaces.
Label
User-facing display name. Can be friendly and descriptive.
Default
Initial value when the HDA is placed in a scene.
Range / Soft Range
Hard range limits valid input; soft range defines the slider's typical span.
Example setup
box_size_x: default 1, soft range 0.1 to 10, hard range 0.01 to 100. This gives a sensible slider while allowing extreme typing if needed.
Common error
Forgetting to Save Node Type: Apply updates the instance but does not persist the HDA definition on disk.
Check
After saving, place a fresh instance of the HDA to verify parameters and organization are stored.

screens.title: Linking Parameters with Channel Expressions
screens.subtitle: Paste Relative References and ch expressions

narration.text: Linking HDA parameters to internal node parameters is the essential plumbing that makes controls functional. The quickest way is using Paste Relative References: copy a parameter inside a node, then paste the reference from the HDA parameter to the internal parameter and Houdini writes the channel call that references the HDA control. Conceptually, the channel expression asks for the value of a named parameter on a parent operator. You can also type the expression manually when needed. Use the channel function ch to reference a parameter by name on a parent level. When you want a float specifically, Houdini often handles conversions, but you can be explicit with type-specific functions when necessary. A concrete example: create a float named box_size on the HDA, copy the internal Box SOP size channel, and paste a relative reference so the Box reads the HDA value. A common misconception is that a single expression will magically reshape different kinds of inputs. You must match data kinds: reference floats to float channels and integers to integer inputs or convert inside the expression. When a parameter is a vector, you can reference individual components or build a composite expression to supply all components. Practice: add a box_size float, paste relative references into sizex, sizey, and sizez, then change the slider and observe live updates. Did you type the parameter name correctly? That spelling is frequently the cause of a broken link.

keyIdea.title: Expressions are connections
keyIdea.text: Paste relative references or type channel expressions to make internal parameters respond to HDA controls; ensure types match.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Channel Expressions
How it works

Copy a parameter from an internal node, then paste the relative reference from your HDA parameter. Houdini writes the channel reference so the internal parameter reads the HDA control at runtime.

Manual example (visual code)
ch("../box_size")
ch("../box_size_x")
ch("../box_size_y")
Use Paste Relative References to avoid typing mistakes. The path goes up to the HDA where the parameter is defined.
Example scenario
Create float box_size on the HDA. Inside the HDA, paste relative references into the Box SOP size channels. When you move the slider, the geometry updates in the scene.
Common pitfalls
  • Spelling errors in the parameter name break the reference. Verify the operator name exactly.
  • Wrong data type: linking a string to a float input causes errors or silent failures.
  • Vector parameters require either individual components or a constructed vector expression.
Try this
Create box_size, then paste relative references into sizex, sizey, sizez. Change box_size and confirm geometry responds. If it does not, re-check the parameter name and type.
Key Takeaway

Paste Relative References whenever possible and ensure parameter names and types match to create reliable links.

screens.title: Expression Types and When to Use Them
screens.subtitle: ch, chf, chi, chs and combining expressions

narration.text: Houdini provides channel functions that target different data types. The basic ch function reads a channel and often auto-detects the type. There are also explicit variants: chf for float, chi for integer, and chs for string. Use ch when you want concise references and Houdini's type inference is sufficient. Use the specific form when you need strict typing or clarity in your expression. A typical case: an integer parameter controlling the number of copies should be linked with an integer-aware expression so rounding or conversion doesn't introduce errors. Another scenario is composing expressions: you can multiply the channel result by a constant or combine multiple channels, for example doubling a size value inside the internal parameter. A common misconception is that these functions change the stored type of the parameter; they only affect how the expression reads or casts the value at runtime. If you need vector components, reference individual channels or construct a vector from separate ch calls. Concrete example: use chi for a fence post count linked to a Copy to Points node, because the number of copies is a whole number. Always test and, when in doubt, prefer explicit functions to avoid subtle conversion problems. Closing question: which function will be safest when linking an HDA integer parameter to a node expecting an integer?

keyIdea.title: Match types explicitly
keyIdea.text: Use type-specific channel functions when linking across different data kinds to avoid conversion errors.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Expression Types
Quick comparison
ch
Generic channel reference. Houdini tries to infer type.
chf / chi / chs
Type-specific: float, integer, and string. Use when you need explicit casting or safety.
When to use which
  • Counts and indices: use chi.
  • Continuous scales: chf or ch.
  • Names or file paths: chs for strings.
Practical examples
Fence posts
Use an Integer parameter and link it with an integer-aware expression for the Copy to Points node's number of copies.
Vector fields
When internal parameter expects a vector, supply components individually or construct a vector from multiple channel calls.
Tip
If you are unsure, test with ch first and switch to chf or chi to remove ambiguity in edge cases.

screens.title: Organizing the HDA Interface
screens.subtitle: Folders, tabs, and separators for clarity

narration.text: A clear interface improves an HDA's usability. The Parameter Interface editor allows folders and separators to group related controls and tabs to split large sets of parameters. Use a simple folder to make a collapsible group for related controls like all the box size and deformation parameters, or create a tab when a set of controls belongs to a distinct mode or workflow. Separators are lightweight and effective for breaking a long list within a folder into smaller logical chunks. When naming folders and labels, think like a user: group parameters by intent rather than by internal node. For example, make a Box Controls folder containing size and extrusion sliders, and a Surface folder for mountain noise and displacement settings. A common misconception is that tabs should be used for every group; overusing tabs can hide important parameters. Prefer folders or separators for related controls that should remain visible by default. Also consider default collapsed state for advanced groups. Concrete practice: create a folder named box_controls, drag the size and extrude parameters inside, and choose Simple so it is collapsible. A neat interface lowers the cognitive load and increases adoption by other artists.

keyIdea.title: Group by intent
keyIdea.text: Organize parameters into folders and tabs that reflect user workflows, not internal node structure.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Organizing the HDA Interface
UI Elements
Folder (Simple)
Collapsible group for a set of related parameters like box size and extrude.
Tab
Creates a separate tab page; use for distinct workflows, not minor groupings.
Separator
Visual divider to break up parameter lists inside folders or tabs.
Design pattern

Group by what the user wants to change. Example groups: Transform, Geometry, Deformation, Output. Avoid grouping by node names.

Example: Box Controls folder
Create a folder named box_controls, label it Box Controls, and drag box_size_x, box_size_y, box_size_z, extrude_dist, mountain_height into it.
Visibility tip
Keep frequently used controls visible by default; collapse advanced or debugging groups.
Key Takeaway

Organize controls around user tasks, not internal structure, and prefer folders and separators to maintain visibility.

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough uses the cohortia_simple_box HDA to practice the full workflow. Start by right-clicking the HDA instance and choose Type Properties, then the Parameters tab. From the left pane drag three Float parameters to the right and name them box_size_x, box_size_y, box_size_z with labels Size X, Size Y, Size Z. Set each default to 1 and soft range from 0.1 to 10. Next, add a float named extrude_dist with default 0.1 and soft range 0.01 to 1, and another float named mountain_height default 0.5 with soft range 0 to 2. Create a Folder, name it box_controls and label Box Controls; drag all these parameters into that folder. Click Apply and Accept to update the instance. Now dive inside the HDA, select the Box SOP and for sizex, sizey, sizez either right-click and Paste Relative References from the HDA parameters or manually type a channel reference that points up to the HDA parameter. Repeat for PolyExtrude distance and Mountain height. Finally, go back up, interact with the sliders, and observe geometry updates. If nothing changes, check parameter names, expression paths, and data types. Save the node type to persist your work.

keyIdea.title: Practice the full loop
keyIdea.text: Perform the add-configure-link-test-save sequence on a sample HDA to build muscle memory and confirm persistence.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Box HDA Walkthrough
Steps
  1. Add floats: box_size_x, box_size_y, box_size_z (default 1, soft range 0.1–10).
  2. Add extrude_dist (default 0.1, soft 0.01–1) and mountain_height (default 0.5, soft 0–2).
  3. Create folder box_controls and move parameters into it.
  4. Apply changes, dive inside HDA, paste relative references into internal SOP parameters.
  5. Test sliders and Save Node Type to persist edits.
Checkpoint
After saving, create a new instance and confirm parameters and folder structure appear as expected.
Example expressions
When Paste Relative References is used, Houdini writes the necessary channel calls. If typing manually, ensure the expression points up into the HDA to find the parameter by its internal name.
Troubleshoot
  • Broken link? Re-check parameter name spelling and the relative path level.
  • Type mismatch? Confirm the HDA parameter kind matches the internal input.
  • Not persisted? Ensure you selected Save Node Type on the HDA node after Apply and Accept.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Parameter Linking
screens.subtitle: Check paths, names, and data types

narration.text: When an exposed parameter does not seem to affect an internal node, methodical checks usually reveal the cause. First, verify the expression path. Relative references traverse the node hierarchy; one level up is typically used. If you manually typed the reference, ensure you referenced the correct relative path level. Second, confirm that the operator name—the internal parameter name—is spelled exactly the same. A typographical error in the name is a common cause of a silent failure. Third, check data types. Linking a string to a numeric input or a single float to an expected vector will produce errors or unexpected behavior. If you need to feed a vector, reference each component individually or construct a vector expression that assembles components from separate channels. Fourth, remember to Apply and Accept to update the instance, and then right-click the HDA node and Save Node Type to persist the definition to disk. A frequent real-world issue is expecting Apply to save the HDA definition; Apply only updates the instance. If your interface reverts the next session, you likely forgot to Save Node Type. For debugging, temporarily set simple numeric defaults and watch whether they appear on the internal node. This helps isolate whether the problem is a path, a name, or a type mismatch.

keyIdea.title: Debug systematically
keyIdea.text: Check path levels, exact parameter names, matching data types, and remember to save the node type after changes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Troubleshooting
Checklist to debug a non-responsive parameter
  • Verify the expression path level; adjust ../ or ../../ if needed.
  • Confirm the internal operator name matches the HDA parameter name exactly.
  • Ensure data types match; convert or use explicit functions for integers or strings.
  • Apply and then Save Node Type so changes persist to disk.
Diagnostic tips
Set a visible default value and inspect the internal node to see if the expression appears.
If a vector is required, try pasting references into each component to observe behavior.
Remember: Apply modifies the instance only; Save Node Type writes the HDA definition to disk.

screens.title: Quick Assessment and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Questions to verify understanding and maintainability

narration.text: After completing the lab, verify your understanding with a few practical checks and follow best practices that keep HDAs robust. First, questions: can you choose the correct parameter type for a given control, such as Integer for counts, Float for sizes, or Toggle for on/off flags? Can you write a channel reference that points to a parent-level parameter and name it correctly? Can you organize parameters into folders and check that the folder collapses and expands as expected? Second, best practices: prefer concise internal names and friendly labels, set sensible defaults and soft ranges, limit the public surface to meaningful controls, group by user intent, and always save the node type after applying changes. Third, documentation: include brief parameter tooltips or descriptive labels where helpful so other artists quickly understand what each slider controls. A common maintenance mistake is leaving debugging parameters exposed; move those into a collapsed Advanced folder. Finally, test by creating a fresh instance of the HDA and manipulating exposed controls; if everything updates and the UI persists after restarting the session, your HDA is ready for sharing.

keyIdea.title: Verify and document
keyIdea.text: Use small tests and clear naming to confirm links work, and document parameters so others can use your HDA correctly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Assessment & Best Practices
Quick assessment
  • Select correct parameter types for given scenarios and explain why.
  • Create a channel expression that links an HDA parameter to an internal node and demonstrate it working.
  • Organize at least five parameters into a folder and justify the grouping.
Best practice
Keep the public interface small and focused; document unusual parameters with labels or descriptions.
Maintenance
Move debugging or low-level controls into a collapsed Advanced folder to avoid user confusion.
Key Takeaway

Small, well-documented interfaces are more likely to be used and maintained. Test with fresh instances and save the node type.

narration.text: These concise concept cards summarize the chapter. Parameters are the public controls you expose so users can modify behavior without opening the node graph. The Parameter Interface editor is the tool where you add and configure those controls, set names, labels, defaults, and ranges. Operator names are the internal identifiers you use in expressions; labels are the friendly names artists see. Expressions like the channel reference let internal nodes read the HDA's parameters. Folders and separators organize controls so the interface is clear. Keep this set of concepts in mind when designing and testing HDAs: choose a minimal public surface, match types, test links, and save the node type so your definition persists. These habits turn a private node network into a reliable, shareable asset. Key Concepts means expose meaningful parameters, link them reliably, organize the ui, and save the asset to make it reusable.. In practical terms, what to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Core summary
keyIdea.text: Expose meaningful parameters, link them reliably, organize the UI, and save the asset to make it reusable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts
Parameters
User-facing controls exposed on an HDA.
Parameter Interface Editor
Tool to add and configure parameters, folders and separators.
Expressions
Channel references that connect HDA parameters to internal nodes.
Takeaway
Well-designed interfaces expose meaningful parameters, use clear names, match types, are organized, and are saved to persist across sessions.

narration.text: Keep these three concise reminders in mind. First, operator names are the internal keys used by expressions; use concise, no-space names for reliable linking. Second, data types matter: choose Integer for counts, Float for continuous values, and String for paths; mismatches cause errors or silent failures. Third, save your node type: Apply updates the instance but does not write the HDA definition to disk. Forgetting to save is the reason many interface edits disappear between sessions. These three points capture the most common pitfalls and the simplest habits that make your HDAs dependable for other artists. What to Remember means name clearly, match types, and save the definition to make your hda stable and shareable.. In practical terms, three compact concept reminders. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Quick Reminders
Operator Name
Internal identifier for expressions; keep concise.
Data Types
Match types to inputs: integer for counts, float for sizes, string for paths.
Save Node Type
Apply affects the instance; Save Node Type writes the HDA definition to disk.
Final takeaway
Clear names, matched types, and saving your work are the smallest habits that yield the most reliable HDAs.
